lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnosis, Complications, Ketoacidosis and Hypoglycaemia

blocks.text: A 52-year-old taxi driver is sent to the clinic after an optician noticed retinal haemorrhages. He has no symptoms, but his fasting glucose is 7.6 mmol/L. By contrast, a 17-year-old student is brought to the emergency department breathing deeply, vomiting and drowsy, with a blood glucose of 31 mmol/L. Both have diabetes, but the diseases, timelines and emergencies are very different.

blocks.markdown: **Diabetes mellitus** is chronic hyperglycaemia from absent or ineffective insulin. Insulin, made by pancreatic beta cells, lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake into muscle and fat and suppressing hepatic glucose output and lipolysis. **Type 1 diabetes** is autoimmune destruction of beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency; it presents typically in children and young adults, with weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia and a tendency to ketosis, and is positive for islet autoantibodies (for example anti-GAD). **Type 2 diabetes** is insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency, associated with obesity, older age and family history; it is often found incidentally or from complications, and ketosis is uncommon.

blocks.title: Diagnostic criteria (WHO and NICE aligned)
blocks.text: Diabetes is diagnosed by: fasting plasma glucose 7.0 mmol/L or above; or random or 2-hour post-glucose-load plasma glucose 11.1 mmol/L or above; or HbA1c 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or above. In a symptomatic person one abnormal result is enough; in an asymptomatic person the abnormal result must be confirmed on a second occasion. HbA1c should not be used where red cell turnover is altered (for example haemolysis, recent transfusion) or in suspected type 1 disease with rapid onset.

rows: Child or young adult, over weeks
Lifestyle, metformin and other agents; insulin later if needed
blocks.caption: Comparison of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

blocks.title: Applying the criteria
blocks.prompt: A 49-year-old woman with no symptoms has a routine HbA1c of 53 mmol/mol. Can you diagnose diabetes?

steps.text: 53 mmol/mol is above the 48 mmol/mol threshold, so the result is in the diabetic range.
She is asymptomatic, so one abnormal result is not enough on its own.
Repeat the HbA1c (or a fasting glucose) on another occasion. If it is again at or above the threshold, diabetes is confirmed.

blocks.answer: Not yet; confirm with a second abnormal test because she has no symptoms.

blocks.markdown: **Complications.** Chronic hyperglycaemia damages small and large vessels. *Microvascular*: retinopathy (leading cause of blindness in working-age adults; annual retinal screening by digital photography), nephropathy (first sign is persistently raised urinary albumin:creatinine ratio, then falling eGFR; annual ACR and eGFR), and neuropathy (distal symmetrical sensory loss in a glove-and-stocking pattern, autonomic dysfunction; annual foot examination with 10 g monofilament and vibration testing). *Macrovascular*: coronary artery disease, stroke and peripheral arterial disease, driven by hyperglycaemia plus hypertension, dyslipidaemia and obesity. Neuropathy with ischaemia leads to painless foot ulcers, infection and amputation. Blood pressure, lipids and smoking are managed alongside glucose.

**Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)** is the emergency of insulin deficiency. Without insulin, glucose cannot enter cells, the liver makes glucose, and fat breakdown produces ketones, which are acids. The result is hyperglycaemia, ketosis (blood ketones 3.0 mmol/L or above) and metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L), with osmotic diuresis causing profound dehydration. Patients have abdominal pain, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing and a fruity (acetone) breath. The acid load widens the **anion gap**.

blocks.caption: Anion gap in mmol/L (potassium omitted); a raised gap indicates unmeasured acid anions such as ketones or lactate.

blocks.title: DKA: the numbers
blocks.prompt: A 65 kg patient has Na 136, Cl 100, HCO3 10 mmol/L. Calculate the anion gap and the starting insulin rate if a fixed-rate infusion of 0.1 units/kg/h is used.

steps.text: 26 mmol/L is raised (a typical reference interval is about 8 to 16), supporting a ketotic acidosis.

items: Fluid: intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride to restore circulating volume, the first priority.
Insulin: fixed-rate intravenous infusion (0.1 units/kg/h) to switch off ketogenesis; add glucose when blood glucose falls below about 14 mmol/L so insulin can continue.

Potassium: total body potassium is depleted even if serum potassium is high at presentation, and insulin drives potassium into cells; monitor closely and replace once potassium is below about 5.5 mmol/L.
Find and treat the precipitant (infection, missed insulin, new diagnosis, myocardial infarction).

Hypoglycaemia: capillary glucose below 4.0 mmol/L. If conscious, 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate; if unconscious or unable to swallow, intravenous glucose (for example 10% glucose) or intramuscular glucagon, then longer-acting carbohydrate and a search for the cause.

blocks.title: Do not stop insulin in DKA while ketones persist
blocks.text: Insulin is needed to switch off ketone production, and the infusion is continued with dextrose added when glucose falls. Stopping it early leaves the patient in ketoacidosis.

points: Diabetes is diagnosed by fasting glucose 7.0 mmol/L or more, random or 2-hour glucose 11.1 mmol/L or more, or HbA1c 48 mmol/mol or more; asymptomatic cases need confirmation.
Type 1 is autoimmune insulin deficiency with ketosis; type 2 is insulin resistance.
Microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular disease are screened for annually.
DKA is treated with fluids, fixed-rate insulin, potassium monitoring and treatment of the cause; hypoglycaemia is treated with fast carbohydrate, or glucagon or IV glucose if unconscious.

questions.stem: A thin 15-year-old has had three weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss. Capillary glucose is 26 mmol/L with 3+ ketones in urine. Which diagnosis is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: young, lean, rapid onset with ketosis.
distractorRationale.b: Type 2 usually occurs in older, overweight patients without prominent ketosis.
distractorRationale.c: Diabetes insipidus does not cause hyperglycaemia or ketosis.
distractorRationale.d: Primary polydipsia does not raise glucose.

questions.explanation: Rapid weight loss, hyperglycaemia and ketones in a young lean patient point to absolute insulin deficiency from autoimmune beta cell loss. Insulin must be started immediately.

questions.stem: In a patient with classic symptoms (polyuria, thirst, weight loss), which single result is sufficient to diagnose diabetes?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 11.1 mmol/L or above in a symptomatic patient.

questions.explanation: A random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or above diagnoses diabetes when typical symptoms are present, and no repeat is required. The other values are below the diagnostic thresholds.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for eight years has normal blood pressure and creatinine but a persistently raised urinary albumin:creatinine ratio on three samples. What does this represent?

options.text: Early diabetic nephropathy, a microvascular complication

questions.correctOptionText: Early diabetic nephropathy, a microvascular complication

distractorRationale.a: Correct: persistent albuminuria is the earliest clinical marker.
distractorRationale.b: Retinopathy is assessed on retinal photography.
distractorRationale.c: Macrovascular disease includes coronary, cerebral and peripheral arterial disease.

questions.explanation: Glomerular damage from hyperglycaemia first causes persistent albuminuria, before the creatinine rises. This is why the ACR and eGFR are screened annually, so treatment such as blood pressure control with an ACE inhibitor or ARB can start early.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old diabetic man has a painless ulcer under the first metatarsal head, warm dry skin, palpable foot pulses and absent monofilament sensation. What is the dominant underlying cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of protective sensation leads to unnoticed pressure injury.
distractorRationale.b: Ischaemic ulcers are painful with absent pulses and cool pale feet.
distractorRationale.c: Venous ulcers occur near the medial malleolus with varicosities.
distractorRationale.d: Acute ischaemia is painful, pale and pulseless.

questions.explanation: A painless ulcer at a pressure point, with intact pulses and absent monofilament sensation, is a neuropathic ulcer. This is why annual foot checks and footwear education are central to diabetes care.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes has glucose 29 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.6 mmol/L, pH 7.08, and is clinically dehydrated and hypotensive. What is the first priority in management?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride to restore circulating volume

questions.correctOptionText: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride to restore circulating volume

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fluid resuscitation is first, then fixed-rate IV insulin.
distractorRationale.b: Insulin is required but a fixed-rate IV infusion is used, and fluids first.
distractorRationale.c: Bicarbonate is not routinely given and may cause harm.
distractorRationale.d: Oral treatment is inappropriate in DKA, and sulfonylureas do not treat type 1 diabetes.

questions.explanation: DKA causes severe dehydration from osmotic diuresis, so intravenous saline restores perfusion first. A fixed-rate insulin infusion then stops ketogenesis, with potassium monitored throughout.

questions.stem: An 84 kg patient with DKA is started on a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h. Calculate the infusion rate in units per hour.
questions.explanation: The rate is 0.1 units/kg/h x 84 kg = 8.4 units/h. The infusion is continued until ketones and acidosis are resolved, with dextrose added when glucose is below about 14 mmol/L.

questions.stem: A patient with DKA has Na 134 mmol/L, Cl 94 mmol/L and HCO3 9 mmol/L. Calculate the anion gap in mmol/L (potassium excluded).
questions.explanation: The anion gap is Na - (Cl + HCO3) = 134 - (94 + 9) = 31 mmol/L. A markedly raised gap reflects ketone anions replacing bicarbonate, as expected in DKA.

questions.stem: Outline the recognition and the initial treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis, including why potassium needs careful management.
markingGuide: Recognition: hyperglycaemia, ketones 3.0 mmol/L or above, acidosis (pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15)
Symptoms and signs: vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, dehydration, acetone breath
Fixed-rate IV insulin; add glucose when glucose falls
Total body potassium is depleted; insulin shifts K into cells, so hypokalaemia risk; replace potassium with monitoring
Monitor ketones, glucose, pH and electrolytes
questions.explanation: DKA is insulin deficiency with unrestrained ketogenesis, so treatment restores volume, supplies insulin, and corrects electrolytes. Potassium is lost in the osmotic diuresis and falls rapidly once insulin drives it back into cells, which can cause fatal arrhythmias if not replaced.

questions.stem: A man with type 1 diabetes is found sweaty and confused with capillary glucose 2.1 mmol/L. Describe your management for the case where he is conscious and can swallow, and the case where he is unconscious.
markingGuide: Hypoglycaemia defined as glucose below 4.0 mmol/L
Conscious: 15 to 20 g fast-acting oral carbohydrate
Recheck glucose and repeat if still low
Unconscious or unable to swallow: IV glucose (such as 10%) or IM glucagon
Identify the cause (missed meal, excess insulin, exercise, alcohol)
questions.explanation: Hypoglycaemia deprives the brain of glucose, so the principle is rapid restoration by the safest available route. Oral carbohydrate suffices if the patient can swallow, but unconscious patients need intravenous glucose or intramuscular glucagon.

questions.stem: True or false: in a person with type 2 diabetes and no visual symptoms, retinal screening can safely be deferred until symptoms appear.
questions.explanation: Retinopathy is asymptomatic until it is advanced, and treatment is most effective when it is detected early. Annual retinal screening is therefore offered to all people with diabetes irrespective of symptoms.
